summary: Describes a robust method for Path MTU Discovery in which TCP or another packetization layer probes an Internet path with progressively larger packets. It extends RFC 1191 and RFC 1981, which rely on ICMP messages.

eli5.summary: To find the biggest package a road can carry, send larger and larger ones and see which arrive. This does that without depending on warning messages that often get blocked.

questions: what is packetization layer path mtu discovery
how does plpmtud work without icmp
what is an icmp black hole

subtitle: Find the largest packet a path can carry by testing it with bigger packets, instead of trusting ICMP error messages.

tldr.problem: Classical Path MTU Discovery relies on ICMP Packet Too Big messages, and when those messages are not delivered or processed, connections can hang.
tldr.mechanism: TCP or another packetization layer sends progressively larger probe packets, raises its packet size when a probe is acknowledged, and treats the isolated loss of a probe as an MTU limit rather than as congestion.
tldr.outcome: It works with or without ICMP, so it can add black hole recovery to classical discovery or replace it entirely. RFC 8899 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4821 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8899; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Probing Instead of ICMP
sections.content:
RFC 4821 describes Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD), an extension to the Path MTU Discovery methods of RFC 1191 (IPv4) and RFC 1981 (IPv6). Those classical methods rely on ICMP messages. PLPMTUD instead starts with small packets and probes with successively larger ones when no ICMP message arrives.

Classical discovery can fail with connection hangs if an ICMP Packet Too Big (PTB) message is not delivered or processed, a problem described in RFC 2923. The bulk of PLPMTUD runs above IP, in the transport layer (such as TCP) or in whatever protocol decides where packet boundaries fall.

The document does not update RFC 1191 or RFC 1981, but because it works without ICMP it implicitly relaxes some of their requirements. It needs no cooperation from peers: it applies only to senders, so differing implementations do not cause interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: Normally a road sends back a note saying your truck is too big. Notes get lost, so this method just tries bigger and bigger trucks and sees which ones get through.

sections.title: What the Method Requires
sections.content:
The only demand on lower layers is that links enforce their MTU: a link MUST consistently discard packets larger than its rated MTU instead of delivering them unreliably. Hosts SHOULD use IPv4 fragmentation in a mode that mimics IPv6, doing all fragmentation on the host and setting the DF bit on every IPv4 packet, fragments included.

A packetization layer that uses PLPMTUD MUST have a loss reporting mechanism that tells the sender promptly and accurately which packets were lost. Normal congestion control MUST stay in effect, with one exception: when only an isolated probe packet is lost, the usual window or rate reduction SHOULD be suppressed. This suppression is rate limited so it happens less often than the worst-case loss rate of TCP congestion control.

Whenever the MTU is raised, congestion state MUST be rescaled so the window in bytes does not grow. Implementations MUST also let applications send packets larger than the current effective Path MTU but smaller than the first-hop link MTU, so that connectionless protocols and diagnostic tools can probe for themselves.
sections.eli5: The rules are: a door must always turn away boxes that are too big, and you must still slow down when the road is jammed. Only when a single test box goes missing may you skip slowing down.

sections.title: Splitting the Work Across Layers
sections.content:
PLPMTUD is easiest to build by splitting its jobs. The IP layer is the best place to keep shared state, collect ICMP messages, track IP header sizes and manage MTU information from link interfaces. The probing and verification logic is tightly tied to the packetization layer, such as its data recovery and congestion control.

The packetization layer must account for header sizes at every layer between IP and itself, and when it conducts a probe it MUST determine the probe's final size including IP headers. The cached Path MTU SHOULD be stored in the IP layer. An implementation MAY use the destination address as its local representation of a path, storing the minimum value because NATs and other middle boxes can show different PMTUs at one address. Network or subnet numbers MUST NOT be used to represent a path.

The RFC also covers IPsec, which can be treated as part of IP or as part of the packetization layer as long as the accounting is consistent, and multicast, where an implementation MAY keep a single small MTU for all multicast packets it originates.
sections.eli5: One helper keeps the shared notebook of what each road allows. Each delivery team does its own test deliveries and writes the result in that notebook.

sections.title: The Probing Method
sections.content:
The method uses three state variables: search_low (the smallest useful probe size, minus one, which the network is expected to carry), search_high (the greatest useful probe size, expected to be too large) and eff_pmtu (the effective PMTU, the largest non-probe packet allowed). A probe MUST be larger than search_low and no larger than search_high. Each conclusive probe narrows the range.

Initially, search_high SHOULD be the largest packet the flow might support, and search_low is RECOMMENDED to start at a size likely to work nearly everywhere; the RFC says 1024 bytes is probably safe enough. An initial eff_pmtu of 1400 bytes is offered as a good compromise. Probe sizes may come from a binary search, from smaller increments (failed TCP probes cost more than successful ones), or from common sizes such as 1500 bytes for standard Ethernet.

Before probing, the flow MUST have no outstanding probes or losses, the probe timeout must have expired if the last probe failed, the available window must exceed the probe size, and enough data must be available. Once probing has converged, a timer SHOULD be set to restart probing; it MUST NOT be less than 5 minutes and is recommended to be 10 minutes, per RFC 1981.
sections.eli5: You keep two numbers: a size you know works and a size you think is too big. Each test box moves one of them closer to the other until they nearly meet.

sections.title: Probe Results, Black Holes and Verification
sections.content:
A probe ends in one of four ways. On success, search_low is set to the probe size and eff_pmtu is raised if the probe was larger. On failure (only the probe was lost), the loss is not treated as congestion and search_high is set to the probe size minus one. After a failure, PLPMTUD MUST NOT probe again until an interval longer than the expected time between congestion events, with the simplest estimate being as many round trips as the congestion window has packets. A timeout failure merits an interval five times longer. An inconclusive probe, lost together with other packets, changes no state and the same-sized probe is retried once preconditions are met.

A full-stop timeout, where nothing sent after some event is acknowledged, is taken as a significant network event. Without an ICMP explanation, the RECOMMENDED first action is to treat it as an ICMP black hole as defined in RFC 2923. After repeated timeouts, search_low and eff_pmtu SHOULD be halved, with lower bounds of 68 bytes for IPv4 and 1280 bytes for IPv6.

Finally, implementations SHOULD perform MTU verification. If a flow is spread over paths with different MTUs, a probe can succeed yet later full-size packets are lost; with two-way round-robin striping, 50% of them. The RECOMMENDED strategy is to save eff_pmtu before raising it and restore it if loss exceeds a threshold, such as 10% over multiple retransmission timeout intervals.
sections.eli5: If only the test box goes missing, the road is probably too narrow. If lots of things go missing, the road is just busy, so wait and try again. If everything stops, shrink your boxes and start over.

sections.title: Probes in TCP, SCTP and Applications
sections.content:
Each protocol must generate probes its own way. TCP cannot tell padding from data, so it must send extra payload in an over-sized segment, either non-overlapping (a lost probe leaves a gap retransmitted in several smaller segments) or overlapping (the gap equals one current MSS, but successful probes cause duplicate acknowledgments). With overlapping, an implementation SHOULD limit the probe size to three times the current MSS, causing at most 2 duplicate acknowledgments.

SCTP is RECOMMENDED to probe by attaching a padding chunk, the PAD chunk of RFC 4820, to a minimum length HEARTBEAT chunk. It must probe each path to the peer independently.

Datagram protocols that depend on IP fragmentation need an adjunct protocol such as ICMP ECHO or traceroute-style UDP datagrams, and should start with a conservative initial MTU. Applications can implement PLPMTUD themselves with a lightweight echo plus a padding mechanism whose padding is not echoed, which lets them measure each direction separately.
sections.eli5: Different delivery services test differently. One adds empty padding to a small package so a lost test costs nothing. Another has to use real cargo for the test.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that PLPMTUD is at least as secure as the standard procedures of RFC 1191 and RFC 1981. It can be configured to ignore all ICMP messages, globally or per application. In that configuration an attacker would need to identify and cause the loss of probe packets, which reduces performance but less than attacking congestion control by dropping arbitrary packets.

Because protocols may share state, a hostile packetization protocol, particularly an application, could hurt others on the same host by reducing the effective MTU. An untrusted protocol should not be allowed to write to shared state.
sections.eli5: Without trusting any warning notes, a troublemaker would have to catch and steal exactly the test boxes. Just do not let strangers write in the shared notebook.

items.title: search_low
items.text: Smallest useful probe size, minus one. The network is expected to deliver packets of this size.

items.title: eff_pmtu
items.text: Effective PMTU for the flow: the largest non-probe packet permitted for the path.

items.title: search_high
items.text: Greatest useful probe size. Packets of this size are expected to be too large.

viz.caption: HOW EACH PROBE RESULT IS HANDLED (RFC 4821, SECTION 7.6)

cells: Set search_low to the probe size; raise eff_pmtu if smaller
Set search_high to probe size minus one; no congestion reduction
Reduce window; wait five times the failure interval
Probe lost along with other packets
Update nothing; retry the same size when preconditions are met
